title: Element-Specific Visualization of Layer-Parity and Twist-Dependent Magnetism in CrSBr
authors: Aalok Tiwari, Shubhada Patil, Ravi Kumar Bandapelli, Alevtina Smekhova, Abhishek Kumar, Wenhao Liu, I-Hsuan Kao, Zhenhong Cui, Raghvendra Posti, Brandon Tran, Zixin Zhai, Priti Yadav, Sandy Adhitia Ekahana, Alexander X. Gray, Bing Lv, Vivekanand Shukla, Florian Kronast, Simranjeet Singh, Jyoti Katoch
abstract: Van der Waals (vdW) based antiferromagnets (AFMs) are an ideal platform for probing and understanding thickness- and twist-angle-dependent emergent spin phenomena. However, element-specific nanoscale characterization of the spin structure in atomically thin vdW-based AFMs systems and layer-parity effects remain elusive, making them crucial for both fundamental insight into low-dimensional magnetism and the rational design of spintronic devices based on these materials. Here, we utilize X-ray magnetic circular and linear dichroisms paired with photoemission electron microscopy to resolve the magnetic order in atomically thin CrSBr. Our comprehensive measurements reveal CrSBr magnetic structure at the nanoscale and its dependence on the layer number, surface encapsulation, temperature, and applied field. Moreover, in the orthogonally twisted bilayer configuration, obtained by twisting two CrSBr ferromagnetic monolayers by 90$^\circ$, the magnetic easy axis fundamentally differs from the individual monolayers, unlocking a new pathway for moiré magnetism.
summary: This work provides element-specific visualization of magnetism in few-layer $	ext{CrSBr}$ using XMCD/XLD-PEEM. It reveals that magnetic order is critically dependent on the layer parity and that twisting the layers fundamentally alters the magnetic anisotropy, opening avenues for designing novel moiré spintronic devices.
main_problem: The study addresses the lack of element-specific, nanoscale characterization of spin structure and layer-parity effects in atomically thin van der Waals (vdW) antiferromagnets.
main_result: The magnetic order is found to be strongly dependent on layer parity, with odd layers exhibiting net magnetization while even layers remain compensated AFM. Furthermore, the twist angle significantly modifies the magnetic anisotropy energy (MAE), suggesting novel moiré magnetism pathways.
method: The research combines advanced experimental techniques like X-ray Magnetic Circular/Linear Dichroism Photoemission Electron Microscopy (XMCD/XLD-PEEM) with theoretical calculations using DFT and Green's function methods to model exchange interactions.
model_or_system: The physical system is atomically thin $	ext{CrSBr}$ in various layer numbers ($1	ext{L}-4	ext{L}$) and twisted bilayer configurations. Theoretical modeling utilizes the Heisenberg Hamiltonian and calculates MAE using the force theorem, incorporating spin-orbit coupling.
key_observables: XMCD asymmetry (magnetic moments), XLD contrast (crystal field effects/anisotropy), Net magnetization direction, Magnetic Anisotropy Energy (MAE), Exchange coupling constants ($J_{ij}$).
important_parameters: Layer number (parity dependence), Twist angle ($	heta$), Temperature ($50	ext{ K}$ to $200	ext{ K}$), External magnetic field strength.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed magnetism is governed by intrinsic layer-dependent coupling mechanisms, and DFT calculations provide an accurate description of exchange interactions across different lattice parameters/twists.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate graphene encapsulation effects on XMCD, layer-by-layer magnetic switching behavior (odd vs. even layers), and how the $	ext{XMCD}$ signal is suppressed or altered in orthogonally twisted bilayer regions based on the azimuthal angle ($\phi$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for nanoscale characterization to presenting experimental evidence of layer-parity dependence, then detailing the unique magnetic response observed in twisted bilayers, and finally supporting these findings with detailed DFT calculations of exchange interactions and MAE.
why_interesting: While primarily condensed matter magnetism, the study's focus on emergent phenomena (moiré magnetism) and the use of advanced spectroscopic probes to map spin structure at interfaces are highly relevant to understanding quantum materials for future quantum technologies.
